# Fimbl

> Fimbl is a modern AI calorie counter, weight loss app and food diary for iPhone and iPad (iOS and iPadOS 26 or later), made by AppRise Ventures Oy in Espoo, Finland. Snap a meal for calories and macros in seconds, follow a daily calorie goal at a realistic pace, keep your weight trend next to private progress photos, and talk it through with an AI coach that reads your own meals, moods and weigh-ins. Available in English, German and Finnish. Free to download with no ads; Fimbl Premium adds AI and depth features.

## What Fimbl does

Fimbl is built around one loop: log what you eat in seconds, check in on how you feel, and let your own patterns show one small thing to change. Its promise is that people keep going instead of starting over.

- Calorie plan: a daily goal from six short questions, at a gentle pace of about 0.5 kg a week or a faster one of about 1 kg a week, to lose, keep or gain weight; the faster plan is off if it would go below what the body needs at rest (free)
- Start without an account: log the first meal right away, then six short questions make the plan and show how that meal fits it (free)
- Food diary with search, barcode scanning, recents, same as yesterday, saved meals, multi-select with undo, and macros and macro goals (free)
- Check-ins before and after meals on hunger, fullness and feelings, plus daily mood; the first personal pattern found in your own check-ins, like which meals leave you with more energy (free)
- Guided First Week: seven days, one small step a day (free)
- Your story, after the first week: write why you started and add the people cheering you on (also a Home Screen widget), keep each week with one card and a minute of answers, and look back on a mosaic of weeks, then and now, a monthly look-back and letters to your future self (free)
- Graded meals: calorie numbers step back and each food gets a simple balance mark (free); Premium adds an AI grade per food with the reason, tips and swaps
- Guided progress photos (front, side, back, face) that stay on the iPhone: never uploaded to Fimbl's servers, never used for AI, never in iCloud backups (free)
- Body notes for symptoms, mood and the menstrual cycle in one calendar; period days stay in Apple Health on the iPhone and never reach Fimbl's servers (free)
- Weight trend, streaks, goals, milestone share cards, Apple Health (reads steps, energy, workouts and smart-scale weigh-ins; writes weight and each meal's energy and macros), Today and check-in widgets, Shortcuts, CSV export (free)
- AI photo and text meal logging: 3 free, then free on iPhones with Apple Intelligence (iOS 27), read by Apple's model on Private Cloud Compute
- Premium: photo scans beyond the free ones, voice logging, AI grades, weekly AI reflections and a coach, every pattern Fimbl finds, recipes from Reels, TikToks and YouTube Shorts, healthier product swaps, more widgets and streak restore. Yearly with a 7-day free trial, or monthly
- AI is optional. Premium AI and the free first tries go through Fimbl's servers to Google's Gemini API, with only what the feature needs and never name or email. Fimbl does not train AI models on user data

## Who Fimbl suits

- People on iPhone or iPad looking for a modern calorie counter: photo, text, voice, barcode and search logging, no ads, and the first meal logged before any account
- People who want to lose weight in one app: calorie goal, macros, weight trend, progress photos and a coach
- People looking for an AI nutrition or weight loss coach that reads their own food log, check-ins and weigh-ins (the coach is part of Premium; the first weekly reflection is free)
- People who want progress photos for weight loss without uploading them anywhere
- People who have quit calorie counting before and want numbers to be optional, or a reason to keep going after week two

## When another app fits better

- Android or web: MyFitnessPal, Cronometer or Lose It!
- Vitamins and minerals in detail: Cronometer
- Calorie targets that adapt automatically: MacroFactor
- The largest branded and restaurant food database: MyFitnessPal
- Workout programmes: Fitbod or Google Health Coach. Fimbl's coach is about eating and habits and doesn't write training plans
- A human coach: Noom (US)
- Medical support, including eating disorders: a healthcare professional

> The full text of the English articles on fimbl.app. Finnish and German versions are listed in llms.txt.

# The best weight loss apps in 2026, compared

URL: https://fimbl.app/blog/best-weight-loss-apps/
Published: 2026-11-06 · Updated: 2026-11-06 · By Kasper Koskenvirta

> An app can help with four things when you're losing weight: showing what you eat, setting a realistic pace, showing change the scale misses, and keeping you going in week three. We compared Fimbl, Noom, MyFitnessPal, Lose It!, MacroFactor, Cronometer and YAZIO on all four.

Most weight loss apps get the first week right. You scan your breakfast, the number goes down, a ring fills up. Then week three arrives, with a birthday, a bad night's sleep and a scale that hasn't moved in nine days. The best weight loss app isn't the one with the cleverest first week. It's the one you're still opening after that.

 The short answer

For most people on iPhone, Fimbl is our pick for losing weight: an AI calorie counter that reads your meals from a photo, a plan at a realistic pace, private progress photos next to your weight trend, and a coach that reads your own days. The diary, barcode scanner, macro goals and progress photos are free, with no ads. If you need something specific, these are strong too:

- Noom for a structured programme with lessons, and a human coach as a US add-on.
- MacroFactor for calorie targets that adapt to your weight trend every week.
- MyFitnessPal for the biggest food database, on iPhone and Android.
- Lose It! for a simple daily calorie budget.
- Cronometer for vitamins and minerals in detail.
- YAZIO if you want fasting timers next to your food log.

A note on bias. We make Fimbl, so we're not neutral. Every claim about another app was checked against that company's own website, help centre or App Store listing in November 2026, each app gets credit for what it does better than ours, and all sources are listed at the end.

## What a weight loss app actually needs to do

An app can't lose weight for you. It can help with four things, and most apps are only strong at one or two of them.

- Show what you eatA calorie counter you'll actually use, with logging fast enough to survive a busy Tuesday.
- Set a realistic paceA daily target you can live with, based on your body rather than a promise.
- Show real progressA weight trend instead of one morning's number, and progress photos for what the scale misses.
- Keep you goingA coach, a reason and people in your corner for the weeks when motivation is gone.

The first item has the best evidence behind it. Reviews of weight loss research consistently link self-monitoring with losing more weight, and in digital programmes, logging more often goes with better results.[1, 2] Most of that evidence is observational, so it can't prove the logging caused the loss. It does make a practical point, though: the app has to be easy enough to keep using. The other three items are what keep you logging.

## Weight loss apps at a glance

| Feature | Our pick Fimbl | Noom | MyFitnessPal | Lose It! | MacroFactor | Cronometer | YAZIO |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Free to use | Yes: Free diary, no ads | Paid plan only: Subscription programme | Yes: With ads | Yes: With ads | Paid plan only: 7-day trial, then paid | Yes: With ads | Yes: With ads |
| AI photo logging | Yes: 3 free, then Premium or Apple Intelligence | Yes: In subscription | Paid plan only: Premium | Paid plan only: Premium | Yes: In subscription | Paid plan only: Gold | Paid plan only: PRO |
| AI coach you can ask | Paid plan only: Premium, reads your meals and moods | Yes: Welli, general answers | Paid plan only: Premium, 5 countries | Not documented | No chat documented: Weekly algorithm check-ins | Paid plan only: Gold, Crono Coach | Not documented |
| Human coach | No | Paid plan only: Premium add-on, US | Not documented | Not documented | Not documented | Not documented | Not documented |
| Progress photos | Yes: Free, guided, stay on your iPhone | Different feature: Body scans instead | Yes: One per weigh-in | Not documented | Paid plan only: In subscription | Yes: "Snapshots" | Not documented |
| Adaptive calorie targets | No: Plan you choose | Yes: Dynamic goals[17] | Not documented | Not documented | Yes: Weekly updates | Not documented | Not documented |
| Hunger & feelings check-ins at meals | Yes: Free | Not documented | Not documented | Not documented | Not documented | Not at meals: Daily mood & energy | Not at meals: PRO mood diary |

For barcode scanners and the other logging details, our [calorie counter comparison](https://fimbl.app/blog/best-calorie-tracker-apps/) goes row by row.

## The apps, and who each one suits

 Best structured programme

### Noom

Less a tracker than a programme, built around psychology lessons, with AI food logging and body scans. Its AI assistant Welli answers general questions any time, and new US members can add a Premium tier with a human 1:1 coach who replies within 24 hours on business days.[8, 9]

Keep in mind: it's a subscription programme rather than a free tool, and the human coach is US-only.

 Best adaptive targets

### MacroFactor

Its algorithm estimates what you really burn from your weight trend and logged food, then adjusts your calorie and macro targets every week, without scolding you for imperfect days. AI photo logging and progress photos are included.[14]

Keep in mind: no free tier, just a 7-day trial, and no hunger or feelings check-ins.

 Best for the biggest database

### MyFitnessPal

The default name in calorie counting. If a branded food exists, it's probably in there. Since June 2026 Premium subscribers in five countries also get an AI Coach that reads their logs.[10, 11]

Keep in mind: barcode scanning, meal scan, voice logging and ad-free use are all part of Premium.

 Best simple calorie budget

### Lose It!

Tell it your goal and it builds a daily calorie budget and a weight loss schedule. Clean and familiar, and it has been helping people count since 2008.[12]

Keep in mind: its App Store listing puts barcode scanning, photo logging and voice logging under Premium, and the free version shows ads.

 Best for nutrient detail

### Cronometer

More than 95 vitamins and minerals from a curated, verified database, with a free barcode scanner. Useful if you're losing weight and want to be sure you aren't short on anything. Gold adds photo and voice logging and Crono Coach.[13, 15]

Keep in mind: the free version shows ads, and the detail can feel like a lab report if you simply want to eat a little less.

 Best with fasting

### YAZIO

A German calorie counter with a free barcode scanner and popular intermittent fasting timers, available on iPhone and Android.[16]

Keep in mind: the free version shows ads, and photo logging, the mood diary and most fasting plans are part of PRO.

 Best for losing weight and keeping going, on iPhone

### Fimbl

A modern AI calorie counter for iPhone and iPad that covers all four jobs in one app: snap a meal for calories and macros, follow a plan at a gentle pace, see your weight trend next to guided progress photos, and talk it through with a coach that knows your days. The diary, barcode scanner, macro goals and progress photos are free, with no ads.

Keep in mind: iPhone and iPad only, a smaller food database than MyFitnessPal, no adaptive targets, and photo scans beyond the free ones and the coach are part of Premium.

## How fast should you lose weight?

The UK's National Health Service gives a clear number: aim to lose 0.5 to 1 kg (1 to 2 lb) a week. It also notes that losing just 5 to 10% of your body weight can improve your health.[3] For someone who weighs 90 kg, that first goal is 4.5 to 9 kg, not a whole new body.

In Fimbl, six short questions turn into a daily calorie goal at one of two paces. A gentle plan is about 500 kcal a day under what your body uses, and a faster one is about 1,000 kcal. With roughly 7,700 kcal in a kilogram of body weight, that's about 0.5 or 1 kg a week. If the faster plan would take you below what your body needs at rest, Fimbl turns it off. Bodies adapt as weight changes, so real progress is usually slower than the formula, and that's normal rather than failure.

 Free A trend instead of one bad morning Log your weight, or let weigh-ins arrive from your smart scale through Apple Health. The trend line shows where you're really heading, and your goal stays in view.

- Calorie goal and macro goals for free
- Exercise isn't added to your budget, so your plan stays steady

## Why progress photos help when the scale won't

The scale can stall while your body changes. Weight naturally rises over the weekend and falls during the week, as a study of 1,421 adults showed.[4] And when you train while eating less, you can build muscle as you lose fat: in one four-week trial of intense training, a calorie deficit and higher protein, participants gained 1.2 kg of lean mass while losing 4.8 kg of fat.[5] The scale showed 3.6 kg. The body changed by six.

That's why progress photos belong in a weight loss app rather than a separate one. They answer the question the scale can't, on exactly the days you're tempted to quit. The catch is that they only work if every photo is taken the same way, and they're among the most private pictures on your phone. Our [progress photo app comparison](https://fimbl.app/blog/best-progress-photo-apps/) looks at how each app handles both.

 Free Before and after, with your weight next to it Fimbl's camera lines you up the same way every time and can take the photo itself. Compare any two days side by side or with a swipe, or play a time-lapse. Your photos stay on your iPhone: never uploaded to our servers, never used for AI and never in iCloud backups. Shown with Fimbl's demo account. The person and photos are AI-generated examples, not a real customer.

Photos and numbers should inform you, not judge you. Repeatedly checking your body can increase body dissatisfaction, especially for people who already worry about how they look.[7] Every week or two is plenty. If thoughts about food or your body take up much of your day, a doctor or an eating-disorder service can help. Fimbl isn't a medical tool or a treatment for eating disorders, and you should talk to a doctor before big changes if you're pregnant, under 18, have a medical condition or take medication that affects your weight.

## The part most apps skip: week three

Almost every "best weight loss app" list ranks databases and AI accuracy. But if you've tried before, a missing food probably isn't why you stopped. Motivation simply ran out, usually around the time the first results slowed down.

What helps at that point is other people. In a classic trial of 166 adults, 66% of those who joined with friends and were given social support strategies kept off all their lost weight over the next six months, compared with 24% of those who joined alone with standard treatment.[6] An app can't recreate that, and we wouldn't claim it does. It can keep the idea in front of you, though.

Weight loss rarely fails on the good days. An app earns its place on the day you'd rather not open it.

-

Your why and your cheerleadersAfter your first week, write down why you started and add photos of the people cheering you on. Both can live on your Home Screen, right when a day gets hard. Free.

-

A coach that knows your weekA weekly reflection connects food, mood and energy, and your coach answers questions from your own days. Your first reflection is free, and the coach is part of Premium.

Fimbl also starts small on purpose. You can log your first meal before making an account, and the First Week is seven days with one small step a day. Miss a day? That's fine. Just don't miss two. If you're curious how AI coaches differ, we compare them in our [guide to AI fitness and nutrition coaches](https://fimbl.app/blog/best-ai-fitness-coach-apps/).

## Where Fimbl isn't the best choice

- You use Android or want a web app. Fimbl is iPhone and iPad only. MyFitnessPal, Cronometer, Lose It! and YAZIO are all on Android.
- You want lessons and a human coach. Noom's programme is built for that, and Fimbl doesn't have human coaches.
- You want targets that adjust themselves. MacroFactor does this better. Fimbl's plan stays where you set it.
- You eat at many US restaurant chains. MyFitnessPal's database is hard to beat for branded and restaurant items.
- You're using weight loss medication. Your prescriber comes first, and some programmes, such as Noom's in the US, are built around it. Fimbl doesn't offer medical support.

 Our pick

### Fimbl: lose weight without starting over

Snap your meals, follow a pace you can live with, watch your trend and your photos change, and keep your why close when the scale goes quiet. It's the weight loss app we built for the weeks after week two.

- AI calorie counter with 3 free photo scans
- Free macro goals and private progress photos
- No ads, and no account needed to start

 [Get Fimbl free](https://apps.apple.com/app/id6443701726)

## How to choose in one minute

-

Start with your phone. On Android, narrow it to Noom, MyFitnessPal, Lose It!, MacroFactor, Cronometer or YAZIO. On iPhone, everything here is open to you.

-

Decide how much structure you want. A full programme with lessons points to Noom. A tool you steer yourself points to Fimbl, Lose It! or MyFitnessPal.

-

Think about what made you stop last time. Typing fatigue calls for photo logging. A stuck scale calls for a trend and progress photos. Lost motivation calls for a coach and a reason to keep going.

-

Check what's free. Make sure what you'll use every day isn't behind a paywall, and that the free version doesn't fill your diary with ads.

Then give it three real weeks, including a bad one. The right app is the one that's still on your home screen afterwards.

## Questions, answered

### What is the best app for weight loss?

It depends on how you like to work. On iPhone, we recommend Fimbl for most people: an AI calorie counter with a realistic plan, a weight trend, private progress photos and a coach that reads your own days. Noom is the strongest structured programme, MacroFactor has the best adaptive calorie targets, and MyFitnessPal has the largest food database.

### What is the best free weight loss app?

Fimbl's free version has no ads and includes the food diary, barcode scanner, a calorie plan, macro goals, weight trend, check-ins and progress photos, plus 3 AI photo scans. It's iPhone and iPad only. On Android, Cronometer and YAZIO have free barcode scanners, and MyFitnessPal and Lose It! offer free calorie budgets, all with ads.

### Do calorie counting apps work for weight loss?

They can help. Reviews of weight loss research consistently link self-monitoring what you eat with losing more weight, and logging more often goes with better results, though most of this evidence is observational. Being consistent matters more than being exact, so choose an app that's quick enough to keep using.

### Which weight loss app has progress photos?

Fimbl has free guided progress photos stored only on your iPhone, with side-by-side and swipe compare, a time-lapse and your weight alongside. MyFitnessPal lets you add one photo per weigh-in, MacroFactor includes front, side and back photos in its subscription, and Cronometer has Snapshots. See our full progress photo app comparison.

### How much weight is it safe to lose in a month?

The NHS suggests aiming for 0.5 to 1 kg (1 to 2 lb) a week, which works out at roughly 2 to 4 kg a month. Progress usually slows as your body adapts. If you're pregnant, under 18, have a medical condition, take medication that affects your weight or have a history of disordered eating, talk to a doctor first.

### Is Fimbl good for weight loss?

Yes, if you're on iPhone or iPad and want to steer it yourself. Six short questions set a daily calorie goal at a gentle pace of about 0.5 kg a week or a faster one of about 1 kg a week, and Fimbl turns the faster plan off if it would go below what your body needs at rest. It adds photo calorie scans, macro goals, a weight trend, progress photos and a coach. It isn't a medical programme and doesn't offer human coaches.

### Why has my weight stopped dropping?

Weight naturally moves through the week, and water, food and new muscle can all hide fat loss for a while. Your body also uses less energy as you get lighter, so progress slows over time. Look at the trend over several weeks along with progress photos and how your clothes fit before changing your plan.

# The best AI fitness coach apps in 2026, and what each one really coaches

URL: https://fimbl.app/blog/best-ai-fitness-coach-apps/
Published: 2026-11-06 · Updated: 2026-11-06 · By Kasper Koskenvirta

> Workouts, sleep or what's on your plate? Fimbl, MyFitnessPal, Cronometer, Noom, Google Health Coach, WHOOP, Fitbod and MacroFactor compared: what each AI coach can actually see, what it costs to use and who it suits.

Everything has a coach now: your calorie counter, your watch, your workout log. In about a year, "AI coach" went from a rare feature to a headline on the App Store pages of some of the biggest health apps. What that headline doesn't tell you is what the coach can actually see, and that decides whether it's talking about you or about people in general.

 The short answer

The best AI fitness coach depends on what you want coached. For losing weight through what you eat on iPhone, Fimbl is our pick: its coach reads your meals, moods, weigh-ins and activity, and connects them to why you eat the way you do. For other goals:

- Google Health Coach for all-round fitness, sleep and wellbeing with a Fitbit or Pixel Watch.
- Fitbod for AI-generated strength workouts.
- WHOOP Coach for recovery and strain, if you wear a WHOOP.
- MyFitnessPal Coach for nutrition advice on top of the biggest food database.
- Noom for an AI assistant plus a real human coach, in the US.
- MacroFactor for a weekly algorithm that adjusts your calories and macros.

A note on bias. We make Fimbl, and its coach is an eating and habits coach, not a personal trainer. Every claim about another app was checked against that company's own website, help centre, App Store listing or a named news report in November 2026. "Not documented" means we couldn't find the feature there, not that it definitely doesn't exist.

## "AI fitness coach" can mean three different things

Search for an AI fitness coach and you'll get three kinds of app under one label. Knowing which one you need saves you from paying for the wrong coach.

- Workout coachesBuild and adjust your training plan. Fitbod is the classic example. They rarely know what you ate.
- Body-data coachesRead a wearable's sleep, strain and recovery data. Think WHOOP Coach and Google Health Coach.
- Eating coachesRead your food log and goals. Fimbl, MyFitnessPal, Cronometer and Noom sit here, each in its own way.

If your goal is building muscle or running faster, start with the first two. If your goal is losing weight, you want a coach that can see your food, because a coach that can't see your plate can only talk in generalities.

## AI coaches compared

| Knows your hunger and feelings at meals | Yes: From your check-ins | Not documented | Not documented | Not documented | Not documented | Not documented | Not documented | Not documented |
| Workout plans | No: Reads Apple Health activity | Answers only: Answers workout questions | Not documented | Paid plan only: Premium add-on, US | Yes: Weekly plan | Daily targets: Daily strain target | Yes: Core feature | Not documented |

## The coaches, and who each one suits

 Best all-round health coach

### Google Health Coach

Built with Gemini, it aims to be a fitness trainer, sleep coach and wellbeing adviser in one. It builds a weekly workout plan, reads your sleep, and analyses photos of your meals. The Fitbit app is now Google Health, on iPhone and Android.[5, 6]

Keep in mind: it needs Google Health Premium, is available only in certain countries, and launched first for Fitbit and Pixel Watch owners.

 Best for strength workouts

### Fitbod

AI-generated gym workouts that balance your exercises, track muscle recovery and learn from your edits. If what you want is someone to tell you what to lift today, this is the one to try.[7]

Keep in mind: a subscription after a free trial, and its listing doesn't document food logging or a chat coach.

 Best for recovery data

### WHOOP Coach

Ask questions and get on-demand answers based on your own biometric data: sleep, strain, recovery and stress. Hard to match if you're training for something specific and already wear the strap.[8]

Keep in mind: the app requires a WHOOP wearable and membership, and it isn't built around what you eat.

 Best on top of a huge database

### MyFitnessPal Coach

Launched in June 2026, Coach turns your logged meals, goals and habits into nutrition guidance: food swaps, recipes, portion changes and restaurant picks. It can also answer questions about workouts.[3, 4]

Keep in mind: Premium and Premium+ only, in the US, UK, Canada, Australia and New Zealand.

 Best for a real person too

### Noom

Welli, Noom's AI assistant, gives fast, general answers on food, fitness and the programme. New US members can add a Premium tier with a dedicated human coach who checks in weekly, plus meal and exercise plans.[9]

Keep in mind: Premium is billed separately from the Noom Weight subscription and is US-only. Noom describes Welli's answers as general.

 Best for nutrient-minded eaters

### Cronometer Crono Coach

An AI assistant in Cronometer Gold that reviews your diary, nutrient averages and targets to spot patterns, and you can tell it what to watch, like a fibre target. Cronometer says it won't change your diary or targets by itself.[10]

Keep in mind: Gold only, and it's built around nutrition data rather than hunger or mood.

 Best hands-off numbers

### MacroFactor

Less a chat than an algorithm: it estimates your energy use from your weight trend and logged food, and adjusts your calorie and macro targets every week, however closely you followed them.[11]

Keep in mind: no free tier, and no chat coach documented.

 Best AI coach for losing weight through eating, on iPhone

### Fimbl

A coach that knows why, not just how much. It reads your meals, the hunger and feelings you check in with, your mood, weigh-ins and Apple Health activity, finds your own patterns and suggests one small thing to try. The food diary, photo calorie counter and progress photos sit in the same app.

Keep in mind: iPhone and iPad only, the coach is part of Premium, and it doesn't write workout programmes.

## Four questions to ask any AI coach

A confident, friendly answer is the easy part. Any modern AI can produce one. These questions show whether there's substance behind it.

-

What can it actually read? Your food, your workouts, your sleep, how you felt? A coach can only be as personal as what it sees, so look for a clear list.

-

Does it end in something to do? Good coaching narrows things down to one small change you can try this week, not a wall of general advice.

-

Does it know its limits? An AI coach isn't a doctor, dietitian or therapist. It should say so, and point you to a person when it matters.

-

Where does your data go? Food, mood and body data are personal. Ask whether AI is optional, what gets sent, and whether it's used to train models.

## Does AI coaching actually work?

Honestly, it's too early to say much. A 2021 systematic review of AI chatbots for activity, diet and weight loss couldn't reach definitive conclusions, and found only one study that measured weight objectively.[1] A 2023 meta-analysis was more encouraging about chatbots for physical activity, fruit and vegetable intake and sleep, but most of its studies were short and of weak quality, and it didn't look at body weight.[2] We didn't find a large peer-reviewed trial showing that today's generative AI coaches lead to more weight loss.

The better-tested idea is simpler. Self-monitoring is one of the most consistent habits linked to weight loss, so a good way to think about a coach is as a reason to keep logging, and as a way to get something useful back when you do. If you want the bigger picture, see our [weight loss app comparison](https://fimbl.app/blog/best-weight-loss-apps/).

The best coach isn't the one that sounds smartest. It's the one that gives you a reason to come back tomorrow.

## Inside Fimbl's coach

We built Fimbl's coach around one question most calorie counters never ask: why? It works in three steps.

- NoticeLog a meal with a photo, your voice, a barcode or a search, and check in before and after: how hungry you were, how full you got, how you felt. It takes seconds, and you can skip it.
- FindFimbl looks for patterns in your own days, like which meals leave you with more energy or when snacking starts. Your first pattern is free. Every week, a reflection connects food, mood and energy.
- AskAsk your coach about your meals, mood or plan, and the answers come from your own days. It suggests one small thing to try instead of a new regime.

-

A week, read back to youWins, patterns and one gentle focus, written about your week. Your first reflection is free.

-

What other coaches can't seeTen-second check-ins tell your coach how hungry you were and how you felt, not just what you ate.

What the coach sees, and what it never does. When you ask something, your message and the last 14 days of your diary, check-ins, mood, body-note symptoms, weigh-ins and goals go through Fimbl's servers to Google's Gemini API, along with steps and active calories if you've turned on Health sync. Your name, email, period days, Your story and your progress photos are never sent, and we don't train AI models on your data. Everything else in Fimbl works without AI. The [privacy policy](https://fimbl.app/privacy/#ai) explains each feature. The coach offers general guidance and isn't a doctor, dietitian or therapist.

## Can ChatGPT be your fitness coach?

For knowledge, it's very good. A general AI assistant can explain progressive overload, sketch a beginner's gym plan or suggest high-protein lunches, and it's a great place to start. Its limit is that it mostly knows what you tell it. It doesn't log your meals, it doesn't remember to ask on Thursday how Tuesday went, and copying your diary into a chat gets old quickly. Some assistants can now connect to health apps if you allow it, so check what that covers and what happens to your data.

A dedicated coach trades range for context: it can do less, but it already has your week in front of it. Plenty of people will use both, and that's a perfectly good answer.

## Where Fimbl isn't the best choice

- You want a training plan. Fimbl doesn't write workouts. Try Fitbod or Google Health Coach.
- You want advice from your sleep and recovery data. WHOOP and Google Health are built around wearables.
- You want a real person. Noom's Premium tier in the US has human coaches, and a dietitian is better still for medical needs.
- You're on Android. Fimbl is iPhone and iPad only.

 Our pick for eating

### A coach that knows why you eat the way you do

Most coaches can tell you what to change. Fimbl's starts with what's actually going on in your days: your meals, your hunger, your mood, your weight. Then it suggests one small thing to try.

- Answers come from your own days
- Your first pattern and weekly reflection are free
- AI is optional, and never trained on your data

## Questions, answered

### What is the best AI fitness coach app?

It depends on what you want coached. Fitbod is strongest for AI-generated strength workouts, Google Health Coach for all-round fitness and sleep with a Fitbit or Pixel Watch, and WHOOP Coach for recovery data if you wear a WHOOP. For losing weight through what you eat on iPhone, we recommend Fimbl, whose coach reads your meals, check-ins, mood, weigh-ins and activity.

### What is the best AI nutrition coach app?

On iPhone, Fimbl is our pick if you want a coach that looks at why you eat as well as what, because it also knows your hunger and feelings at meals. MyFitnessPal Coach suits people who already use its food database, and Cronometer's Crono Coach suits people focused on vitamins, minerals and nutrient targets.

### What is the best AI coach for weight loss?

Look for a coach that reads your food log and your weight. Fimbl does that on iPhone and iPad, alongside a photo calorie counter, a plan at a gentle pace and private progress photos. Noom is a good choice if you want a structured programme with a human coach in the US, and MacroFactor if you want your calorie targets adjusted automatically every week.

### Is there a free AI fitness coach?

Most personal AI coaches are part of a paid plan, including those from Fimbl, MyFitnessPal, Cronometer and Google Health. Fimbl gives you your first weekly reflection and your first personal pattern for free. Noom says members keep access to Welli without its Premium tier, but Noom itself is a subscription. A general assistant like ChatGPT can answer fitness questions for free, but it mostly knows only what you tell it.

### Can ChatGPT replace a fitness coach?

For general knowledge and simple plans, it can go a long way. It doesn't log your meals or workouts or follow up by itself, though, and it mostly knows only what you share. A dedicated coach has your data in front of it. Neither replaces a doctor, dietitian or qualified trainer when you have a medical condition or an injury.

### Is an AI coach as good as a human coach?

Not for everything. An AI coach is available at any hour, cheaper and good at spotting patterns in your data, but research on AI coaching is still early, and a person is better at accountability, judgement and complex situations. Noom's US Premium tier combines both. If you have a medical condition or a history of disordered eating, please see a professional.

### Does Fimbl's coach make workout plans?

No. Fimbl's coach focuses on eating, habits, mood and weight, and it can take your Apple Health activity into account if you allow it. For a training plan, Fitbod or Google Health Coach are better fits. Fimbl does have simple workout goals and reads your workouts from Apple Health.

### Does Fimbl train AI on my data?

No. Fimbl doesn't train AI models on your data or sell it. When you ask the coach something, the request goes through Fimbl's servers to Google's Gemini API with only what the feature needs, and never your name, email, period days, Your story or progress photos. AI is optional, and everything else in Fimbl works without it.

# What a modern calorie counter does in 2026, and which apps do it

URL: https://fimbl.app/blog/modern-calorie-counter-app/
Published: 2026-11-06 · Updated: 2026-11-06 · By Kasper Koskenvirta

> Photo logging, a coach that reads your data, numbers you can switch off and no ads. Eight things that separate a modern calorie counter from a search box, and how Fimbl, Cal AI, MyFitnessPal, MacroFactor, Lifesum, Lose It! and Cronometer score.

The classic calorie counter is a search box. Type "chicken", choose from forty entries, guess the grams, and do it again six times a day. It works, and plenty of people have lost weight that way. It's also why so many of us have a calorie app we opened for nine days and never again. In the last two years, that has finally started to change.

 The short answer

A modern calorie counter lets you log a meal in seconds from a photo, your voice or a barcode, lets you correct what the AI gets wrong, coaches you from your own data, and doesn't charge you in ads or your privacy. On iPhone, Fimbl is our pick because it does all of that in one app, and it lets you log your first meal before making an account. Other good options:

- Cal AI if you want the simplest possible photo-first tracker.
- MyFitnessPal if you want the classic database with new AI on top.
- MacroFactor if you want targets that adapt to you every week.
- Lifesum if you want AI logging, meal plans and an Android app.

A note on bias. We make Fimbl, and we chose this checklist knowing how Fimbl does on it, so read it with that in mind. Every claim about another app was checked against that company's own website, help centre or App Store listing in November 2026, and sources are listed at the end.

## What changed: the old way and the modern way

| | Classic calorie counter | What to look for now Modern calorie counter |
|---|---|---|
| Logging | Search, pick an entry, enter grams | Photo, voice, text or barcode, in seconds |
| Getting started | Account and a long questionnaire first | Log something first, set up later |
| Feedback | A number and a red bar | A coach that reads your days and suggests one thing |
| Off days | Over budget, in red | Context, and a way to keep going |
| Progress | Today's weight | A trend, plus progress photos |
| Business model | Ads, or a paywall on the basics | No ads, and the basics stay free |
| Privacy | Everything in the company's cloud | The most personal data stays on your phone |

None of this means older apps are bad. Several have added AI features and kept what made them popular, like a huge food database. "Modern" isn't about an app's age. It's about whether using it still feels like homework.

## Eight things a modern calorie counter should do

-

Log from a photo. Snap the plate and get calories, protein, carbs and fat. It's the biggest change in calorie counting in a decade, because mixed meals no longer take ten entries.

-

Understand your voice and plain words. "A chicken wrap and a latte" should be enough.

-

Keep a free barcode scanner. For packaged food, the label beats any AI estimate. It's a basic that shouldn't sit behind a paywall.

-

Let you start in seconds. The first log should come before the long questionnaire and the account.

-

Coach from your data. Not generic tips, but answers based on what you actually ate this week.

-

Make numbers optional. Calories motivate some people and wear others out. A modern app lets you step back without losing your history.

-

Show progress beyond the scale. A weight trend and progress photos, in the same place as your food.

-

Respect you. No ads in your diary, and a clear answer on where your data and photos go.

## How today's apps score

| Feature | Our pick Fimbl | Cal AI | MyFitnessPal | MacroFactor | Lifesum | Lose It! | Cronometer |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Photo logging | Yes: 3 free, then Premium or Apple Intelligence | Paid plan only: Results need a subscription | Paid plan only: Premium | Yes: In subscription | Paid plan only: Premium | Paid plan only: Premium | Paid plan only: Gold |
| Voice logging | Paid plan only: Premium | Not documented | Paid plan only: Premium | Yes: In subscription | Paid plan only: Premium | Paid plan only: Premium | Paid plan only: Gold |
| Free barcode scanner | Yes | In subscription: In subscription | Premium: Premium | In subscription: In subscription | Yes | Premium: Premium | Yes |
| First log before an account | Yes | Not documented | Not documented | Not documented | Not documented | Not documented | Not documented |
| AI coach from your data | Paid plan only: Premium | Not documented | Paid plan only: Premium, 5 countries | No chat documented: Weekly algorithm | Not documented | Not documented | Paid plan only: Gold |
| Numbers optional | Yes: Graded meals, free | Not documented | Not documented | Not documented | Not documented | Not documented | Not documented |
| Progress photos | Yes: Free, guided, stay on your iPhone | Not documented | Yes: One per weigh-in | Paid plan only: In subscription | Not documented | Not documented | Yes: "Snapshots" |
| No ads | Yes: Free & Premium | Yes: None listed | Paid plan only: Premium only | Yes: Never uses ads | Yes: None listed | Paid plan only: Paid only | Paid plan only: Gold only |
| Android | No: iPhone & iPad only | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes |

 Available Paid plan only No, or not documented Checked against each provider's website, help centre and App Store listing, November 2026. Apps change often, so check before you subscribe.

No app ticks every box, including ours: Fimbl has no Android version and keeps voice logging and the coach in Premium. The wider comparison, with what each app is genuinely best at, is in our [calorie counter comparison](https://fimbl.app/blog/best-calorie-tracker-apps/).

## Is photo calorie counting accurate enough?

Accurate enough to be useful, yes. Exact, no. In a 2025 study, the best general-purpose AI models were off by about 36% per photo on average, and they tended to underestimate large portions. The researchers still found them comparable to traditional self-reported food diaries, without the effort.[1] Adding a few words about the meal helps a lot: in a second study, average error fell from about 31% with the photo alone to 24% with a short description.[2]

So a modern calorie counter should treat AI as a very fast first draft. You see the estimate, fix the portion, and save. For packaged food, you scan the barcode instead. Our guide to [AI calorie tracking accuracy](https://fimbl.app/blog/ai-calorie-tracking-accuracy/) covers when to trust each method.

A rough log you keep for three months beats a perfect one you abandon in a week.

Adjust any estimate before you save it. Your first three scans are free, and on iPhones with Apple Intelligence they stay free after that, read by Apple's own model on Private Cloud Compute.

- Free barcode scanner, search and same as yesterday
- Recipes from Reels, TikToks and Shorts in Premium

 Free Log first, set up later Open Fimbl and log what's on your plate right now, with no account and no long questionnaire first. Six short questions then make your plan and show how that meal fits it. Your diary moves to your account whenever you make one.

- Calories, macros and macro goals, free
- Apple Health both ways, plus widgets and Shortcuts

 Free · AI grades in Premium Numbers when you want them Switch to Graded meals and calories step back: each food gets a simple balance mark, and your diary keeps counting in the background. Premium adds an AI grade for each food, the reason behind it, tips and swaps. Our guide to [tracking food without counting calories](https://fimbl.app/blog/track-food-without-counting-calories/) explains the idea.

Add your coach, a weight trend, private progress photos and your why on your Home Screen, and it's the modern calorie counter we wanted for ourselves. For how the pieces work together when your goal is losing weight, see our [weight loss app comparison](https://fimbl.app/blog/best-weight-loss-apps/).

## Should you leave MyFitnessPal?

Only if something is bothering you. If it works for you, keep it: the food database is enormous, it runs on Android and the web, and it now has an AI Coach in Premium.[3, 4] People usually look for a MyFitnessPal alternative for one of three reasons: barcode scanning is a paid feature, the free version shows ads, or the daily numbers have started to feel like a test.

- For a free barcode scanner: Fimbl on iPhone, or Cronometer, Lifesum and YAZIO, which also run on Android.
- For no ads: Fimbl's free version has none, and MacroFactor never uses them but has no free tier.
- For the simplest logging: Cal AI, or Fimbl's photo scan.
- For when numbers feel like a test: Fimbl's Graded meals, which no other app here documents.

## Where Fimbl isn't the best choice

- You use Android or want a web app. Fimbl is iPhone and iPad only.
- You want a huge branded database. Fimbl builds on Open Food Facts, Fineli and USDA data. MyFitnessPal has more branded and restaurant items.
- You track specific vitamins and minerals. Cronometer goes much deeper.
- You want targets that adapt by themselves. MacroFactor's algorithm does this, and Fimbl doesn't.

Fimbl reads your plate in seconds, doesn't need an account to start, shows no ads and gives you a coach that knows why you eat the way you do. When the numbers wear you out, they step back.

- 3 free photo scans and a free barcode scanner

- English, German and Finnish

## Questions, answered

### What is the most modern calorie counter app?

On iPhone, we'd pick Fimbl: photo, voice and text logging, a free barcode scanner, no account needed for your first meal, an AI coach that reads your own days, optional numbers with Graded meals, private progress photos and no ads. Cal AI is the simplest photo-first tracker, and MacroFactor is the most advanced on adaptive targets.

### What is the best AI calorie counter?

It depends on what you want around the scan. Fimbl pairs photo scans with a coach, check-ins and progress photos, with 3 free scans and free scans afterwards on iPhones with Apple Intelligence. Cal AI is built purely around the photo, though its scan results need a subscription. MacroFactor and MyFitnessPal offer AI logging on top of larger tracking tools.

### How accurate are photo calorie counters?

They're rough but useful. In a 2025 study, the best general-purpose AI models were off by about 36% per photo on average, comparable to traditional self-reported diaries, and they tended to underestimate large portions. Describing the meal in a few words improves the estimate, and for packaged food a barcode scan is more reliable.

### Is there a calorie counter without ads?

Yes. Fimbl has no ads in either its free or Premium version. MacroFactor never uses ads but has no free tier, and Lifesum and Cal AI list none. MyFitnessPal, Cronometer, Lose It! and YAZIO show ads in their free versions and remove them with a paid plan.

### Can I use a calorie counter without making an account?

Fimbl lets you log your first meal and use your diary without an account, and it moves to your account whenever you make one. The coach and weekly reflections need a free account so they can remember your weeks. We didn't find this documented for the other apps we compared.

### What is the best modern alternative to MyFitnessPal?

On iPhone, Fimbl is a good alternative if you want a free barcode scanner, no ads, photo logging and a coach. Cronometer suits people who want micronutrient detail and works on Android and the web. MacroFactor suits people who want adaptive targets. If MyFitnessPal's database matters most to you, it's still hard to beat.

### Do I need to count calories to lose weight?

No, though it helps many people see what they're really eating. If numbers wear you out, a calorie counter with a numbers-optional view, like Fimbl's Graded meals, keeps the record without the daily total. There are also other ways to track, such as the plate method and hunger scales, which we cover in our guide to tracking food without counting calories.

# The best calorie tracker apps in 2026, compared side by side

URL: https://fimbl.app/blog/best-calorie-tracker-apps/
Published: 2026-10-17 · Updated: 2026-11-06 · By Kasper Koskenvirta

> Fimbl, MyFitnessPal, Cronometer, MacroFactor, Lose It!, YAZIO, Lifesum and Cal AI side by side: what each one is genuinely best at, what's free, and how to pick the one you'll still open in a month.

Almost every calorie tracker can count. Search a food, scan a barcode, watch a number go down. The real difference shows up later, on the Tuesday you skipped lunch and ate cereal for dinner. Some apps make that day feel like a failure. Others help you understand it. That difference decides whether you're still tracking in a month.

 The short answer

For most people on iPhone who want to lose weight and still be tracking in a month, Fimbl is our top pick: snap a meal for calories and macros, a free barcode scanner, free macro goals and private progress photos, no ads, check-ins on hunger and feelings at every meal, an AI coach that reads your own days (Premium), and Graded meals for when the numbers wear you out. If you need something specific, these are excellent:

- Cronometer for micronutrient detail (95+ vitamins and minerals, free).
- MacroFactor for adaptive calorie and macro targets.
- MyFitnessPal for the biggest food database.
- YAZIO or Lifesum for a free barcode scanner on Android too.
- Cal AI if you only ever want to snap a photo.

A note on bias. We make Fimbl, so we're not neutral observers. Here's how we approached it: every claim about another app was checked against that company's own website, help center or App Store listing in October 2026, each app gets credit for what it does better than ours, and all sources are listed at the end.

## How we compared them

Feature lists are easy to compare and tell you surprisingly little. So alongside the usual checks, we looked at what decides whether a tracker actually helps:

- Speed: how many ways you can log a meal, and how fast each one is.
- What's free: whether the basics (search, barcode, history) work without paying, and whether the free version shows ads.
- The off days: how the app treats you when you go over, skip a day or eat a birthday cake.
- Insight beyond calories: whether it helps you notice hunger, feelings and patterns, not just totals.
- Privacy and reach: ads, data use, platforms and languages.

The last three matter more than they sound. Reviews of weight-management research consistently find that people who keep logging tend to do better, but the evidence is about consistency.[13] The tracker that wins is the one you keep opening.

Two rows stand out. Only Fimbl asks how you feel at the moment you eat, and only Fimbl documents a way to stop seeing calorie numbers without losing your history. Everyone else is, at heart, a very good counter. AI coaches have gone from rare to common in a year too, so it's worth asking what each one actually reads and coaches. We compare them in our [guide to AI fitness and nutrition coaches](https://fimbl.app/blog/best-ai-fitness-coach-apps/).

## What each app is genuinely best at

 Best for the biggest database

### MyFitnessPal

The default name in calorie counting, with more than 20 million foods and links to dozens of apps and devices. Since December 2025 it also owns Cal AI, and since June 2026 Premium includes an AI Coach in the US, UK, Canada, Australia and New Zealand.[17]

Keep in mind: barcode scanning, ad-free use and custom macro goals are part of Premium, and the free version shows ads.

 Best for micronutrients

### Cronometer

The precision tool. It tracks more than 95 vitamins and minerals for free from a curated, verified database, which makes it a favourite of dietitians and anyone managing specific nutrients. Gold adds photo and voice logging and an AI assistant, Crono Coach.

Keep in mind: the free version shows ads, and the level of detail can feel like a lab report if you simply want to eat a little better.

 Best for adaptive macros

### MacroFactor

Its algorithm estimates your energy expenditure from your weight trend and adjusts your targets every week, without scolding you for imperfect days. Great for training goals.

Keep in mind: there's no free tier (a 7-day trial), no web app, and the app is in English and Japanese only.

 Best for a simple calorie budget

### Lose It!

A straightforward daily budget that has been helping people count since 2008. Clean, familiar and easy to start.

Keep in mind: its App Store listing puts barcode scanning and AI logging under Premium, and the free version shows ads.

 Best for European foods

### YAZIO

A German app with a large food database, a free barcode scanner and popular fasting timers, available in 20 languages.

Keep in mind: the free version shows ads, and photo logging, the mood diary and most fasting plans are part of PRO. There's no web version.

 Best for meal plans

### Lifesum

A design-led Swedish app built around healthy eating, with diet programmes, recipes, a free barcode scanner and a simple "Life Score".

Keep in mind: AI tracking, custom macro goals and meal plans are Premium, and micronutrient detail is limited.

 Best for photo-only logging

### Cal AI

Point your camera, get calories and macros. If typing a single food name feels like too much, it's the fastest route from plate to log.

Keep in mind: scan results require a subscription, and it tracks calories and macros only, with nothing on hunger or mood.

 Best for a guided programme

### Noom

Less a tracker than a structured programme, with daily psychology lessons and coaching. Foods are sorted by a colour system based on calorie density.

Keep in mind: it's built around a subscription programme, and its GLP-1 medication offering (Noom Med) is available in the US only.

 Best for a habit that lasts, and understanding why you eat

### Fimbl

A modern photo calorie counter for iPhone and iPad that tracks calories and macros like the others, then adds the part they leave out: how hungry you were, how you felt, and a coach that connects the two. The free version is a complete diary with a barcode scanner, macro goals, private progress photos and no ads. More on why we rank it first below.

Keep in mind: iPhone and iPad only, no micronutrient deep-dive, a smaller food database than MyFitnessPal, and photo scans beyond the free ones and the coach are part of Premium.

## The question most comparisons skip

Most "best calorie app" lists rank database size and AI accuracy. Those matter. But if you've tried tracking before, you probably didn't stop because a food was missing. You stopped because it started to feel like a test you kept failing.

The research backs this up in both directions. Logging what you eat is one of the most reliable habits linked to weight-management success, and more consistent digital tracking goes with better results.[13, 14] Yet in one study, almost half of young adults using healthy-eating and fitness apps described negative experiences such as guilt and feeling controlled.[15] On the other hand, a randomised trial found that a month of calorie tracking didn't raise eating-disorder risk in low-risk students.[16] The takeaway isn't that tracking is bad. It's that how an app makes you feel is part of whether it works.

The best tracker isn't the one with the most foods. It's the one you still open on the day you'd rather not.

## Why Fimbl comes out on top for most people

We built Fimbl around one idea: notice what you eat, understand why, and change one small thing at a time. Here's what that looks like in the app.

 Free It asks how you feel, not just what you ate A ten-second check-in around your meals: how hungry were you, and what were you feeling? Craving, stressed, bored, satisfied. Pick as many as you like, or none. Over a few weeks, the patterns behind your eating start to show.

 Free & Premium Numbers when you want them, grades when you don't Switch to Graded meals and calorie numbers step back: each food gets a simple balance mark, for free. Premium adds an AI grade for every food, the reason behind it, tips and swaps. Fimbl keeps counting quietly in the background, so switching back loses nothing.

Snap your plate or describe it in a few words: your first three are free, and on iPhones with Apple Intelligence they stay free. Put together, that's the difference. Other apps are excellent at telling you what you ate. Fimbl is built to help you understand why, and it stays kind on the days that don't go to plan.

## Where Fimbl isn't the best choice

Every app has limits, Fimbl included. Choose something else if:

- You use Android or want a web app. Fimbl is iPhone and iPad only. MyFitnessPal, Cronometer and Lose It! run on both, and YAZIO and Lifesum on Android.
- You track specific vitamins and minerals. Cronometer's micronutrient detail is in a different league.
- You're dialling in macros for training. MacroFactor's adaptive targets are built for exactly that.
- You eat out at many US chains. MyFitnessPal's database is hard to beat for branded and restaurant items.
- You need medical support. No app replaces a doctor or dietitian. Fimbl isn't a medical tool or a treatment for eating disorders.

## How to choose in two minutes

-

Start with your phone. On Android or the web, narrow it to MyFitnessPal, Cronometer, Lose It!, YAZIO or Lifesum. On iPhone, everything here is open to you.

-

Name what you're really after. Precision (micronutrients, macros for training) points to Cronometer or MacroFactor. A calmer relationship with food and habits that last points to Fimbl.

-

Notice how numbers make you feel. If seeing a calorie total every day motivates you, any counter works. If it makes you anxious, pick an app that lets you step back from numbers without losing track.

-

Check what's free before you commit. Make sure the basics you'll use daily, like barcode scanning, aren't behind a paywall, and that the free version doesn't fill your diary with ads.

Then give it a real week. Not a perfect one, a real one. The right app is the one that's still on your home screen when the week is over.

## Questions, answered

### What is the best calorie tracker app in 2026?

It depends on what you need. On iPhone, we recommend Fimbl for most people who want to lose weight and keep going, because it pairs photo calorie scans, free macro goals and private progress photos with hunger and feelings check-ins and an AI coach that reads your own days. Cronometer is the best choice for detailed micronutrients, MacroFactor for adaptive macro targets, and MyFitnessPal for the largest food database.

### Which calorie counter has a free barcode scanner?

As of October 2026, Fimbl, Cronometer, YAZIO and Lifesum include barcode scanning in their free versions. MyFitnessPal moved barcode scanning to Premium in 2022, and Lose It! lists it as a Premium feature in its App Store description.

### Is there a calorie tracker without ads?

Fimbl has no ads in either its free or Premium version. MacroFactor never uses ads but has no free tier, and Lifesum and Cal AI list no ads. MyFitnessPal, Cronometer, Lose It! and YAZIO show ads in their free versions and remove them with a paid plan.

### Can I track what I eat without seeing calories?

Yes. Fimbl's Graded meals view is free: calorie numbers step back and each food gets a simple balance mark, while Fimbl keeps counting in the background. Premium adds an AI grade for each food with the reason, tips and swaps. You can switch back to numbers at any time. None of the other apps in this comparison document a comparable mode.

### What is a good alternative to MyFitnessPal?

On iPhone, Fimbl is a good alternative if you want free barcode scanning, no ads and a calmer, feelings-aware diary. Cronometer suits people who want micronutrient detail, and YAZIO suits people who want a large European food database on Android as well as iPhone.

### Is calorie counting bad for your mental health?

For many people it's a useful, neutral tool. Some studies link calorie-tracking apps with more eating concern in certain users, while a randomised trial in low-risk students found no increase in eating-disorder risk. If tracking makes you anxious, a numbers-optional approach can help, and if food feels overwhelming, please talk to a healthcare professional.

### Which calorie counter apps have an AI coach?

As of November 2026, Fimbl (Premium), MyFitnessPal (Premium, in five countries) and Cronometer (Gold, called Crono Coach) all document an AI coach you can ask about your own logs. MacroFactor adjusts your targets with a weekly coaching algorithm rather than chat. See our full comparison of AI fitness and nutrition coaches.

### Does Fimbl work on Android?

No. Fimbl is built natively for iPhone and iPad running iOS or iPadOS 26 or later. If you need Android or a web app, MyFitnessPal, Cronometer, Lose It!, YAZIO and Lifesum are available there.

# The best progress photo apps in 2026, compared

URL: https://fimbl.app/blog/best-progress-photo-apps/
Published: 2026-10-19 · Updated: 2026-11-06 · By Kasper Koskenvirta

> The scale can't tell fat from water or muscle. Photos can, if every one is taken the same way. We compared how Fimbl, Progress, Hevy, MacroFactor, MyFitnessPal and Cronometer help you capture, compare and protect your body transformation photos.

Three weeks of eating well, two workouts a week, and the scale says you've lost 300 grams. Your jeans disagree. So does the mirror, on a good day. Progress photos settle the argument, but only if they're taken the same way every time. Most apps hand you a camera and wish you luck. A few actually help you line up the shot.

 The short answer

For documenting a body transformation alongside your food and weight, Fimbl is our pick: guided front, side, back and face photos, live on-device alignment, hands-free auto-capture, side-by-side and swipe compare, a time-lapse, and photos that never leave your iPhone. All of it is free. Other good options:

- Progress if you want a dedicated photo and measurement app with a passcode lock and iCloud sync.
- Hevy if you lift and want photos next to your workout log.
- MacroFactor if you already use it for adaptive macros and want front, side and back slots.

A note on bias. We make Fimbl, and progress photos are one of the features we're proudest of. Every claim about another app was checked against that company's own help centre, privacy policy or App Store listing in October 2026, and "not documented" means we couldn't find the feature there, not that it definitely doesn't exist. Sources are listed at the end.

## Why progress photos beat the scale

The scale measures everything at once: fat, muscle, water, glycogen, last night's salty dinner. That makes it noisy in the short term. In a study of 1,421 adults, weight rose over the weekend and fell during the week as a normal pattern,[1] and a Finnish study of daily weigh-ins concluded the same weekly rhythm should be seen as normal, not as weight gain.[2]

The bigger blind spot is body composition. In a four-week trial combining a calorie deficit, training and a higher-protein diet, participants gained 1.2 kg of lean mass while losing 4.8 kg of fat.[3] The scale showed 3.6 kg. The body changed by six. That's the change photos capture and numbers miss: shoulders, posture, waist, the way a T-shirt sits.

- The scalePrecise, frequent and noisy. Great for long-term trends, poor at telling fat from water or muscle.
- PhotosShow shape and proportions. Only useful if every photo is taken the same way.
- How you feelEnergy, sleep, clothes fitting. The measure most worth listening to, and the one no app can take for you.

## How to take progress photos you can actually compare

A progress photo is only as good as its consistency. Change the distance, the angle or the light, and you're comparing photography, not bodies.

-

Same place, same light. Pick one spot with even, front-facing light. Daylight from a window in front of you works well. Avoid overhead lights that carve shadows.

-

Same time and conditions. Morning, before eating, in similar clothes. Food, water and a pump after training all change how you look.

-

Same distance and height. Prop the phone at chest height, far enough away that your head and feet both fit. A timer beats a mirror selfie every time.

-

Same poses. Front and side at minimum, back if you can. Relaxed, arms slightly away from your body, no sucking in.

-

Same rhythm. Every week or two is plenty. Daily photos show mostly noise, and can turn into checking.

This is exactly where most apps stop helping. Getting steps three and four right by yourself, week after week, is hard. It's the part we built Fimbl's camera around.

## The apps, and who each one suits

 Best dedicated photo app

### Progress

A long-standing body measurement app with front, side and back photos, a "Show Last Photo" overlay, side-by-side compare, and photos encrypted on your device with iCloud sync.[4]

Keep in mind: photos are part of the paid Pro plan, and there's no food diary.

 Best for lifters

### Hevy

A popular workout tracker where you can add a photo with your measurements, line it up with an overlay of your last one and compare it side by side. Photos stay private even if your profile is public.[5]

Keep in mind: one photo per day, so front and side shots need separate days, and full body measurements need Pro.

 Best alongside adaptive macros

### MacroFactor

Front, side and back photo slots, one of each per day, plus before-and-after images you can share. A natural fit if you already use its adaptive calorie targets.[6]

Keep in mind: no free tier, and its privacy notice says data is stored with Google Firebase in the US.[7]

 Simplest photo per weigh-in

### MyFitnessPal

Add one photo with each weigh-in and compare them as a split photo. Simple, and it lives next to the biggest food database around.[8]

Keep in mind: no poses or alignment help, and photos sync to MyFitnessPal's servers.

 A snapshot with your vitals

### Cronometer

"Snapshots" attach a photo to the vitals you log at that moment, next to Cronometer's detailed nutrient tracking.[9]

Keep in mind: it's a photo log rather than a comparison tool: no poses, overlay or compare view.

 Best overall for body transformation

### Fimbl

The only food diary we checked with a guided camera: it finds your body, coaches you into the same position as last time and takes the photo itself. Compare, time-lapse and private, on-device storage are all free.

Keep in mind: iPhone and iPad only, no app lock, and photos stay on that one iPhone: they don't sync to a new phone.

## Inside Fimbl's progress photos

We wanted progress photos to feel like having a patient friend behind the camera. Here's what happens when you take one:

- Line upThe camera finds your body on the device, about eight times a second, and coaches you: step back until your head and feet show, move a little left, lined up with your last photo. Prefer to see it? Toggle a faint overlay of your previous shot.
- CaptureProp your phone up and step back. Once you're in position, a three-second countdown starts and the photo takes itself. Step out of line and it waits for you.
- ComparePhotos are auto-aligned so your body sits in the same place in every frame, whatever your distance from the camera. Compare side by side or swipe between them, or press play for a time-lapse.

 Free in Fimbl Before and after, with the whole story Pick any two photos of the same pose. Fimbl shows the days between them, the weight change, a mini chart of every weigh-in in between and how far you've come towards your goal. Lineup lines at shoulders, waist, hips and knees make small changes easier to see. Shown with Fimbl's demo account. The person and photos are AI-generated examples, not a real customer.

- Front, side, back and face, each as its own series
- Recrop a photo to match, with the other one faintly over it
- Share card for Stories or posts, with weights and dates optional

-

Check it before you keep itHold the new photo to see your previous one in its place, then retake or keep it. Every photo belongs to a weigh-in, so your trend and your pictures always tell the same story.

-

Your whole journey, one swipe awayScrub the strip to move through every weigh-in, see the change since your first photo, or press play for a time-lapse. Meals, mood and activity sit in the same app, so you can see what happened in between.

## Privacy: where your body photos live

Progress photos are among the most personal pictures on your phone, often taken in underwear or less. Where they're stored matters. In 2025, researchers found a fitness app's cloud storage left open to anyone, exposing more than 138,000 users' progress photos.[10] It was closed after it was reported, but the lesson stands: a photo that's never uploaded can't leak from a server.

### How Fimbl stores them

Only on your iPhoneNever uploaded to our servers, never used for AI, and the body detection runs on the device.

Encrypted at restProtected by iOS file encryption and unreadable while your phone is locked.

Out of backups and your camera rollExcluded from iCloud backups and kept out of Photos unless you switch on "Save to Photos".

### What that means for you

They don't follow you to a new phoneBecause they're never backed up, switching phones, deleting the app or signing out removes them.

Want a copy?Turn on "Save to Photos" to keep new shots in your library too. Those copies follow your iCloud Photos settings.

Sharing is your callOnly a share card you create ever leaves your phone, and only when you share it.

### What about AI body-fat scans?

Some apps now estimate body-fat percentage from photos or a short video. Noom's Body Scan, for example, uses technology from Prism Labs and sends the scan for processing.[11, 12] The idea is appealing, but the numbers are rough: an independent study of two smartphone apps found typical errors of 3.9 to 6.2 percentage points of body fat compared with a lab reference.[13] That's the difference between 22% and 28%. For tracking your own change, consistent photos and a weight trend tell you more, and they don't require uploading pictures of your body.

Photos should make you feel more informed, not more critical. Repeatedly checking your body can increase body dissatisfaction, especially for people who already worry about how they look.[14] Take photos every week or two rather than every day, look at them alongside how you feel, and pause if they start to make you anxious. If thoughts about your body or food take up much of your day, a doctor or an eating-disorder service can help. Fimbl isn't a medical tool or a treatment for eating disorders.

-

Need a passcode lock or sync across devices? A dedicated app like Progress, which encrypts photos and syncs through iCloud.

-

Already living in a workout log? Hevy's photo and overlay will fit right into your routine.

-

On Android? Fimbl and Progress are iPhone apps. Whatever you choose, look for two things: an overlay of your last photo, and a clear answer on where your photos are stored.

Whichever you pick, the rule is the same: same spot, same light, same pose, every week or two. And if the scale and the mirror still disagree, remember the study above: six kilograms of change can look like three and a half on the scale. ## Questions, answered

### What is the best app for progress photos?

It depends on what else you track. For progress photos alongside a food diary and weight, Fimbl offers guided front, side, back and face photos, live on-device alignment, auto-capture, side-by-side and swipe compare and a time-lapse, all free and stored only on your iPhone. Progress is a strong dedicated photo app with a passcode lock and iCloud sync, and Hevy suits people who already log workouts.

### How do I take consistent progress photos?

Use the same spot, light, time of day, clothing, camera height and distance every time, and the same poses: front and side at minimum, back if you can. Prop the phone up and use a timer rather than a mirror. An app with an overlay of your last photo, or Fimbl's live alignment guide, makes lining up much easier.

### How often should I take progress photos?

Every one to two weeks is plenty. Daily photos mostly show day-to-day noise such as water and food, and frequent body checking can increase body dissatisfaction for some people. Taking photos together with a weigh-in keeps the rhythm simple.

### Why do I look different but weigh the same?

The scale combines fat, muscle, water and glycogen. Weight naturally rises and falls through the week, and if you're training while eating less you can gain muscle while losing fat. In one trial, people gained 1.2 kg of lean mass while losing 4.8 kg of fat in four weeks, so the scale understated the change. Photos capture shape changes the scale misses.

### Are progress photos in fitness apps private?

It varies. Many apps upload photos to the company's servers or cloud. Others, such as Fimbl, keep them on your phone. In Fimbl, progress photos are never uploaded, never used for AI, encrypted on the device and excluded from iCloud backups. The trade-off is that they don't transfer to a new phone unless you save copies to Photos.

### Can an app measure body fat from a photo?

Some apps estimate it, usually by sending your photos or video to a server for analysis. The estimates are rough: an independent study of two smartphone apps found typical errors of 3.9 to 6.2 percentage points compared with a laboratory method. Consistent photos and a weight trend are more useful for tracking your own change.

### Are Fimbl's progress photos free?

Yes. Capturing, comparing, the time-lapse, recropping and the share card are all part of the free version of Fimbl for iPhone and iPad, with no ads.
